newsitem.title: CHINA: China warns U.S. not to back U.N. rights motion.
newsitem.headline: China warns U.S. not to back U.N. rights motion.

text.p: China warned the United States on Thursday that relations could suffer if it pressed ahead with support for Denmark's decision to censure China's human rights record in the United Nations.
However, the biggest loser would be Denmark, Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a news briefing.
"Sino-U.S. relations have already seen improvements, but the U.S. support of Denmark will, of course, damage bilateral relations," Shen said.
"The U.S. government should resolve this problem from the basis of bilateral relations," he said.

China's response to a U.S. decision to support Denmark's determination to push ahead with a resolution to censure China in the United Nations Human Rights Commission in Geneva this month was unusually restrained, reflecting an improvement in relations.

Both the United States and China have moved painstakingly in recent months to ease strains over disputes ranging from Taiwan to trade and human rights that sent ties plummeting in 1995 and early 1996.

U.S. Vice-President Al Gore visited China last month and reassured Beijing that the administration remained committed to an exchange of visits by President Bill Clinton and China's President Jiang Zemin over the next two years.
Beijing appeared eager to try to limit damage to slowly improving ties as a result of U.S. support for Denmark's decision to press ahead with the U.N. motion to fault China.
However, Beijing lashed out again at Denmark.
"Denmark should consider its national interests and consider seriously the consequences," Shen said.
"Denmark's anti-China motion will eventually become a stone that will fall on its own head," he said.

Denmark has said it is determined to persist, despite splits in the European Union that -- coupled with Washington's delay in deciding to co-sponsor the resolution until after last week's visit to China by Gore -- make it unlikely the resolution will be adopted. Previous attempts to condemn China on human rights in a U.N. resolution following Beijing's bloody 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy protesters have failed. China has rallied enough support each year to block the move.
In its annual human rights report for 1996, the U.S. State Department said China had effectively silenced public dissent by jailing or exiling virtually every active dissident.
However, signs have emerged recently that China may be prepared to engage in bilateral discussion of an issue it has always insisted is purely an internal affair.

China, a focus of controversy over its treatment of dissidents and widespread use of the death penalty, said this week it was ready to sign this year the U.N. International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights.
It kept silent on a similar pact on political freedoms.
In Canberra, Australia said on Thursday it had reached agreement with China for the two countries to establish a formal "bilateral dialogue on human rights".
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen welcomed the agreement. "Australia's decision is very wise," he said.

Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said the agreement, reached in principle with visiting Chinese Justice Minister Xiao Yang on Wednesday, would help achieve progress on human rights in China.
